title: Console walkthrough - Usage analytics & per-route cost breakdown - VelaTech
summary: Redwood AE/SE ran a console walkthrough focused on usage analytics, per-route dashboards, and cost breakdown. VelaTech is evaluating hosted vs dedicated for customer-facing assistants and wants visibility into per-route cost/latency, multi-tenant cost allocation, and compliance for HIPAA-sensitive flows. Next steps: send pricing examples for pilot, share security SOC2 docs and a short guide to per-route tagging, schedule benchmark test for end of May.
next_steps: Maya to send pilot pricing examples and SKU mapping by 2026-05-16
Ethan to share SOC2 + security whitepaper link 2026-05-15
Schedule 1-hour benchmarking session week of 2026-05-25 (owner: Alex)
Provide per-route tagging guide and example dashboard export
action_items: Maya - Send pilot pricing examples and SKU mapping by 2026-05-16
Ethan - Share SOC2, ISO docs and network diagram link by 2026-05-15
Alex - Confirm bench window and sample workload by 2026-05-20
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Can you hear me okay?
[00:02] Alex Morgan: Yep loud and clear, thanks.
[00:08] Maya Chen: Cool. Quick intros, I'm Maya from Redwood, account lead. Ethan here is our solutions engineer who will do the console walkthrough.
[00:15] Ethan Rodriguez: Hi all. I'll jump into the console and show the per-route dashboards, usage analytics, and how we do cost breakdowns. Priya is along for any billing/operator questions.
[00:23] Jules Rivera: Hi, Jules from platform, Samir from security and Cara from product.
[00:29] Ethan Rodriguez: Great. I'll share my screen. Give me one sec.
[00:33] [screen share starts]
[00:36] Ethan Rodriguez: Alright, so this is the Redwood Console. Top left you'll see the date range selector, filters by model, project, and route. We'll click into the VelaTech demo project we've preprovisioned.
[00:48] Ethan Rodriguez: First pane is overall usage. You can see tokens generated, requests per minute, average latency p50/p95, and spend. Notice spend is broken down by model variant and quantization profile.
[01:05] Jules Rivera: Sorry quick Q, how do you attribute costs to our customers? We have multiple tenants in one deployment.
[01:12] Ethan Rodriguez: Good question. We have per-route tagging and per-API-key attribution. You tag routes with tenant IDs and the console will show per-tenant usage and cost allocation. There's an export to CSV for chargeback.
[01:23] Alex Morgan: Are those tags retroactive or do we need to instrument ahead of time?
[01:28] Ethan Rodriguez: We generally need the tags to be present at request time for precise attribution. For historical data we can do heuristic attribution based on API keys and routes but it's less precise.
[01:36] Maya Chen: For a pilot we recommend adding tenant IDs to headers; it's a small change and gives clean per-route granularity.
[01:43] Samir Patel: From compliance side, can we get audited logs for who called what and what prompt was used?
[01:50] Ethan Rodriguez: We keep detailed audit logs; you can configure retention policies. For private Dedicated or Private installs, logs can be forwarded to your SIEM, and payload redaction is supported for PII/HIPAA flows.
[02:03] Samir Patel: And KMS for encryption of cached artifacts?
[02:06] Ethan Rodriguez: Yes we integrate with customer KMS or HSM for key management in Private deployments.
[02:12] Cara Holmes: Back to the dashboard, can you show per-route latency distributions? We care about tail latencies for chat flows.
[02:18] Ethan Rodriguez: Sure. Click into Routes -> Customer Chat. Here you get a histogram of latency, plus p50/p90/p95 and a time series. You can also break it down by model variant, sequence length buckets, and whether KV cache hit or miss.
[02:33] [pause while loading]
[02:35] Ethan Rodriguez: You'll see here that chat route uses rdx-7b-int8 by default, p95 around 620ms, and p99 spikes when long contexts hit. We surface cache hit rate next to that which helps explain cost/latency tradeoffs.
[02:48] Alex Morgan: That rdx-7b-int8—is that Redwood's optimized quantized variant?
[02:52] Ethan Rodriguez: Yep, that's our 7B int8 profile; good middle ground for cost and latency. You can pin routes to model profiles per environment, or have a routing policy that falls back to hosted larger models during bursts.
[03:04] Jules Rivera: How do you compute cost per route? Is it just tokens * model unit price?
[03:09] Ethan Rodriguez: It's tokens times unit price plus infra overhead. Basically we model per-token execution cost per model/profile and then allocate overhead (GPU reservation, data transfer) proportionally to usage. The console shows the raw token cost and an allocated overhead line item so you can see full landed cost.
[03:25] Maya Chen: We also show amortized reserved capacity cost for Dedicated pools if you're on committed capacity; that helps you decide whether to move high-volume routes to Dedicated.
[03:34] Samir Patel: Can you show an example of a high-volume route and how the recommendation engine suggests batching/quantization changes?
[03:40] Ethan Rodriguez: Yes. Under Optimize -> Recommendations I've got a sample workload. For route Orders-API we recommend enabling prefix caching and switching quantization to int8 4k profile; predicted cost drop by ~37% with minimal change in quality per our eval metrics.
[03:54] Alex Morgan: How confident are those quality estimates? We can't degrade response quality for the support assistant.
[03:59] Ethan Rodriguez: Confidence is based on internal evals against your uploaded prompt/response set. If you provide a 200-500 prompt set we can run a sensitivity eval showing delta in BLEU/EMB-sim/ROC depending on metric you prefer. We surface thresholds and flag potential regressions.
[04:16] Cara Holmes: Is there an easy way for product to tag example prompts to a route so we can run regressions over time?
[04:21] Ethan Rodriguez: Absolutely — the console has an Evaluations tab where you can upload a prompt set and map them to routes. You get periodic regression alerts and can pin a baseline model.
[04:30] [15-second pause while Ethan scrolls]
[04:45] Ethan Rodriguez: Now I'll open the Cost Breakdown for the last 30 days. Top section shows spend by project, below that is by route. See the pie for top 10 routes. You can click a route to see token counts, average request size, cache hit rate, and cost per 1k requests.
[05:03] Jules Rivera: Do you show per-region costs? We have multi-region failover and want to understand egress/region pricing impact.
[05:09] Ethan Rodriguez: Yes region is a first-class filter. We show per-region infra premium and data transfer; you can compare same route across regions and see delta.
[05:19] Samir Patel: Where does the console pull pricing from? Is it fixed or can we override with our reserved rates?
[05:25] Ethan Rodriguez: Defaults come from Redwood's catalog and infra model, but you can override pricing per-customer or per-contract so accounting reflects your committed reserved rates.
[05:34] Alex Morgan: Great. On SLA — if we hit p95 above our target do you provide automated routing fallback?
[05:40] Ethan Rodriguez: Yes you can create routing policies: route by latency threshold, region, or cost. Fallbacks to a cheaper/higher throughput model are configurable with circuit-breaker style rules and automatic reverts.
[05:51] Cara Holmes: For reporting, can we export dashboards or hook into BI tools?
[05:55] Ethan Rodriguez: Export to CSV and JSON is available. We also have a metrics export that integrates with DataDog or Prometheus for deeper BI.
[06:03] [screen scroll]
[06:06] Ethan Rodriguez: I'll demo a sample chargeback export. Here we select project VelaTech, date range, group by tenant tag, and you get a CSV that includes tokens, token-cost, infra overhead, and total charge.
[06:19] Jules Rivera: Nice. About tokenization differences — do you normalize across models? We use different tokenization depending on model which affects per-token math.
[06:27] Ethan Rodriguez: Good point. We compute cost in raw model tokens; for chargeback we also provide normalized token equivalents so you can map to a canonical token unit for billing if you prefer.
[06:36] Samir Patel: On security — you mentioned payload redaction earlier. If we use redaction, how do evaluations that need full prompts work?
[06:44] Ethan Rodriguez: You can opt-in to storing evaluation payloads unredacted in a restricted bucket for audit purposes, or have them hashed and linked to an internal key store accessible only by compliance. It depends on your policy.
[06:58] Maya Chen: Quick commercial note — during pilot we often enable hosted API with per-route tagging so you can get immediate analytics without needing Dedicated setup. Then we run a short benchmark to see whether Dedicated reserved capacity yields material savings.
[07:11] Alex Morgan: What's a typical breakpoint where Dedicated becomes cheaper?
[07:14] Maya Chen: It depends on peak throughput and burstiness. As a rule of thumb, if sustained throughput exceeds ~200-400k tokens/hour on consistent peaks, Dedicated can be favorable, but we'll model it for you.
[07:26] [screen transition]
[07:28] Ethan Rodriguez: I'll show the Routing & Rollouts panel. You can create a canary for a new model variant for a route, send 5% traffic, and watch metrics side-by-side: latency, cost, cache hit, and quality regressions. If quality drops or latency increases beyond thresholds, auto-rollback triggers.
[07:46] Cara Holmes: Does the console support experiment tagging for A/B testing?
[07:49] Ethan Rodriguez: Yes experiments are first-class. You can label variants and get split metrics and a statistical test of delta for your chosen metric (e.g., user satisfaction proxy).
[07:59] [small cross talk]
[08:02] Jules Rivera: For our infra team, are there alerts we can subscribe to for cost spikes? We had a surprise in another vendor where a misrouted job created a huge bill.
[08:10] Ethan Rodriguez: You can set budget alerts per-project/route that notify via Slack, email, or webhook when spend exceeds thresholds. There's also anomaly detection on token spikes that flags unusual patterns.
[08:22] Samir Patel: Can RBAC restrict who can view raw prompts in the console?
[08:26] Ethan Rodriguez: Yes RBAC is granular: you can restrict prompt viewing, audit log access, deploy permissions, and cost export. Integrates with SAML/SCIM for sync with your IdP.
[08:36] Alex Morgan: For the benchmarking you mentioned — what do you need from us?
[08:40] Ethan Rodriguez: Sample prompt set (100-300 prompts) per route, expected concurrency, typical context size, and your success metric (latency SLO or quality threshold). We'll run both hosted and dedicated test runs and share a cost/perf report.
[08:55] Alex Morgan: We can compile that. Anything special for HIPAA-sensitive prompts?
[08:59] Ethan Rodriguez: Mark them and we will run those in Private deployment or with payload redaction and KMS enabled.
[09:06] [pause]
[09:10] Maya Chen: I'll summarize: we'll send pilot pricing examples and sku mappings, Ethan sends SOC2/security docs and a quick per-route tagging guide, Alex will propose bench dates. We'll plan a 1-hour bench session week of 2026-05-25. Anything else?
[09:23] Cara Holmes: Could you include a sample exported chargeback CSV so our finance team can see the format?
[09:27] Maya Chen: Yes we'll attach that.
[09:29] Samir Patel: Also need the network diagram for Dedicated/private deployment.
[09:33] Ethan Rodriguez: I'll include the network diagram and recommended VPC peering setup.
[09:38] Alex Morgan: Sounds good. A couple small notes — when you showed p95 spikes during long contexts, can we set a warning earlier than auto-rollback, like just an alert so product can triage?
[09:47] Ethan Rodriguez: Absolutely. Alerts are separate from routing policies; you can have soft alerts and hard thresholds.
[09:53] [brief pause]
[09:56] Maya Chen: Any final questions?
[09:58] Jules Rivera: One more on quotas — can we reserve capacity for internal-critical routes?
[10:02] Ethan Rodriguez: Yes you can create capacity reservations for routes and guarantee minimum concurrency on Dedicated.
[10:09] Alex Morgan: Perfect. Thanks all. Looking forward to the bench.
[10:12] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with docs and next steps.
[10:16] [meeting ends]

Notes on transcript quality: auto-transcription had typical mislabels and occasional missed words; speaker turns captured but sometimes overlapping.
